title: The struck-down obscenity provision that's still being misused
p1:
Imagine being booked under a law that the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional years ago.

Sounds impossible? It has happened in India.

And the provision at the centre of this controversy is Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
p2:
Here's the surprising part: Section 66A was struck down by the Supreme Court on 24 March 2015 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

It criminalised sending allegedly offensive or menacing messages online, with punishment of up to three years' imprisonment.

The problem? Terms like 'offensive' and 'annoying' were dangerously vague, giving authorities excessive power over online expression.

One important clarification: Section 66A was not technically an obscenity provision. It dealt with offensive online communications. Obscenity-related offences are separately addressed under provisions such as Section 67 of the IT Act.
p3:
Yet, striking down a law doesn't automatically erase every reference to it from official records.

In October 2022, the Supreme Court went further. It directed that no citizen could be prosecuted under Section 66A and that references to it in pending proceedings must be deleted.

The practical takeaway: If an FIR invokes Section 66A, remember that it has no legal force. A different, independently applicable offence may still be investigated, but Section 66A itself cannot be used.
conclusion: How can a provision declared unconstitutional in 2015 continue appearing in criminal proceedings years later? Is the bigger problem outdated legal records, inadequate police training, or weak implementation of judicial decisions?
